entries.title: Deglaze and the pan sauce
entries.say: As it reads: deglaze, pan sauce.
entries.summary: A pan sauce is made in minutes in the pan a piece of meat or fish was seared in: the browned juices are lifted with wine or stock, reduced, enriched and finished, so nothing the searing made goes to waste.
entries.guest: A pan sauce is made from the browned juices left in the pan, with shallot, wine and stock. Our Poussin à la Moutarde carries its cousin, a tangy, rich mustard cream sauce.

paras: To deglaze, déglacer in French, is to pour liquid into a hot pan after searing and scrape up the browned film stuck to its base. American kitchens call that film the fond; French cooks usually call it the sucs, and to them fond chiefly means a base, as in a stock. It is the meat's browned juice, and it dissolves readily, so the pan that cooked the steak becomes the start of its sauce.
A pan sauce is the quickest sauce in the classical kitchen: made to order, in the same pan, while the meat rests. It turns a seared piece into a finished dish.

Sear in a stainless or carbon steel pan; non-stick will not build a fond. Lift the meat out to rest and look at the pan: chestnut to mahogany is right, but black is burnt and bitter, so start again in a clean pan. Pour off all but about 15 ml (1 tbsp) of fat, lower the heat and sweat a finely chopped shallot for a minute, soft and without colour.

Deglaze: pour in the wine, stock or spirit and scrape hard with a flat wooden spatula as it bubbles; the fond lifts within seconds. Wine is the usual choice, because its acid and alcohol draw out flavours that water leaves behind. Reduce it almost dry, au sec, so its raw taste cooks away. A spirit such as brandy goes in off the flame; lighting it is taught with flambé.

Add stock, or stock and cream, and reduce again to nappe, when the sauce coats the back of a spoon. Tip in the meat's resting juices. Off the heat, swirl in cold butter a piece at a time until the sauce turns glossy; why it works is taught with monter au beurre. Season and serve at once.

For two portions: one shallot, about 30 g (1 oz); 120 ml (1/2 cup) of wine reduced to a spoonful; 180 to 240 ml (3/4 to 1 cup) of stock reduced by half; and 30 g (1 oz) of cold butter. That gives about 120 ml (1/2 cup) of sauce. Use unsalted stock and season at the end, because reduction concentrates salt along with flavour.

Change the liquid and the finish and the method gives a family. White wine, shallot and chicken stock suit chicken, veal and fish; red wine and brown stock, mounted with butter, suit steak and duck; cream reduced in the pan makes a cream sauce.

The mustard cream of poulet à la moutarde, the Burgundian bistro chicken, is the model of the cream branch: shallot softened in butter, white wine reduced, cream simmered to nappe, and Dijon mustard stirred in off the heat. Boiled, mustard loses its bite and can turn bitter, so it goes in last and the sauce is not boiled again.

Hence the rule: cream sauces may boil; butter-finished sauces must not. Heavy cream, at 36 per cent fat or more, holds its fat in protected globules and can be boiled hard to reduce it. Light cream, half-and-half and milk curdle, especially with acid in the pan. A butter-mounted sauce breaks at the boil, so the butter goes in last, off the heat.

Bitter: the fond burnt black, or garlic browned too far; start again in a clean pan. Sharp and raw: the wine was not reduced before the stock. Thin: reduce it longer. Sticky: loosen it with stock. Greasy: the fat was not poured off, or the butter boiled. Salty: a salted stock reduced too far; add unsalted stock or a little cream.

At Brennan's the Poussin à la Moutarde carries a mustard cream sauce in the Burgundian bistro tradition, where shallot is softened in butter, white wine reduced, cream simmered and mustard stirred in off the heat so it keeps its bite; how tonight's sauce is built is the chef's detail. The hen is brined in sweet tea and fried, and comes with turnips and shallots: a crisp Southern bird under a French bistro sauce.

Describe the mustard cream as tangy and rich, a French bistro sauce over a crisp Southern bird. The poussin is a whole small bird and may have bones, so say so. Questions about the cream, the butter or the fried coating go to the service note and the kitchen.

faults.cause: The fond burnt black, or garlic browned too far.
faults.fix: Nothing hides it: start the sauce again in a clean pan.

faults.cause: The wine was not reduced before the stock went in.
faults.fix: Next time reduce the wine almost dry first; now, simmer a little longer and finish with butter.
Reduce until it coats the back of a spoon, then finish.

faults.cause: The searing fat was not poured off, or the butter boiled after mounting.
faults.fix: Skim the fat, bring the base back to nappe and mount it again off the heat.

faults.cause: A salted stock reduced too far.
faults.fix: Loosen with unsalted stock or a little cream, and season only at the end next time.

cards.front: What is the fond, and why does a pan sauce need it?
cards.back: The browned film of meat juices stuck to the pan after searing. It carries concentrated, roasted flavour and dissolves in liquid to become the base of the sauce.

cards.front: What do French cooks call the browned bits, and what does fond mean to them?
cards.back: Les sucs. To a French cook fond chiefly means a base, as in a stock; American kitchens use fond for the browned film itself.

cards.front: Why pour off most of the fat before deglazing?
cards.back: Fat does not dissolve the fond and only makes the sauce greasy; about 15 ml (1 tbsp) is kept to sweat the shallot.

cards.front: Why is wine the usual liquid for deglazing?
cards.back: Its acid and alcohol draw out flavours that water alone leaves behind. It is reduced almost dry so its raw taste cooks away.

cards.front: The fond has burnt black. What do you do?
cards.back: Start the sauce in a clean pan: a burnt fond makes the sauce bitter, and nothing added afterwards hides it.

cards.front: What is the order of a classic pan sauce?
cards.back: Pour off the fat, sweat the shallot, deglaze and reduce almost dry, add stock and reduce to nappe, add the resting juices, mount with cold butter off the heat, season.

cards.front: How do you know a pan sauce has reduced to nappe?
cards.back: It coats the back of a spoon, and a finger drawn through it leaves a clean line that holds.

cards.front: Why may a cream sauce boil when a butter-finished sauce may not?
cards.back: Heavy cream keeps its fat in protected globules, so it reduces at a boil without splitting; a butter-mounted sauce is a fragile emulsion that breaks if it boils.

cards.front: What is a working pan sauce for two portions?
cards.back: One shallot, 120 ml (1/2 cup) of wine reduced almost dry, 180 to 240 ml (3/4 to 1 cup) of stock reduced by half, and 30 g (1 oz) of cold butter.

cards.front: Why does the mustard go into a mustard cream off the heat?
cards.back: Boiling dulls the mustard's bite and can make it bitter, so it is stirred in last and the sauce is not boiled again.

cards.front: Why use unsalted stock and season a pan sauce only at the end?
cards.back: Reduction concentrates salt along with flavour, so a stock seasoned at the start can leave the finished sauce too salty.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dish carries a mustard cream sauce, and what does it go with?
cards.back: The Poussin à la Moutarde: a mustard cream after the Burgundian bistro poulet à la moutarde, over a sweet tea-brined, fried Cornish hen with turnips and shallots.

questions.q: In an American kitchen, what is the fond of a pan sauce?
questions.answer: The browned juices stuck to the pan after searing
distractors: The fat poured off before deglazing
A roux cooked to a dark brown
The cold butter swirled into the sauce at the very end
questions.why: The fond is the browned film the searing leaves behind; liquid dissolves it, and it becomes the base of the sauce.

questions.q: Before you deglaze, what should happen to the fat left from searing?
questions.answer: Pour off all but about 15 ml (1 tbsp)
distractors: Leave all of it in the pan for richness
Whisk it into the wine
Brown it until it smokes
questions.why: Fat cannot dissolve the fond and only makes the sauce greasy; a spoonful is kept to sweat the shallot.

questions.q: After searing, the fond in the pan is black. What is the right move?
questions.answer: Start the sauce in a clean pan
distractors: Deglaze with extra wine to mask it
Add sugar to balance the bitterness
Mount it with more butter
questions.why: A burnt fond tastes bitter, and no wine, sugar or butter added afterwards hides it.

questions.q: Why is the wine reduced almost dry before the stock goes in?
questions.answer: So its raw, sharp taste cooks away
distractors: So the alcohol thickens the sauce
So the fond sticks harder to the pan
So the butter can go in earlier
questions.why: Reducing the wine au sec drives off its harshness and concentrates its flavour; skipped, the sauce tastes sharp and raw.

questions.q: What tells you a pan sauce has reduced to nappe?
questions.answer: It coats a spoon and holds a line
distractors: The pan is completely dry
The sauce sets solid when cold
The surface stops bubbling
questions.why: Nappe means the sauce coats the back of a spoon; a line drawn through it holds instead of flooding back.

questions.q: Which of these sauces may be boiled to reduce it?
questions.answer: A heavy cream sauce
distractors: A sauce already mounted with butter
A sauce finished with mustard
A beurre blanc
questions.why: Heavy cream's fat sits in protected globules and survives a boil; butter emulsions break, and boiled mustard loses its bite.

questions.q: In the mustard cream of poulet à la moutarde, when does the mustard go in?
questions.answer: Last, stirred in off the heat
distractors: First, fried with the shallot
With the wine, to reduce with it
Boiled with the cream to thicken it
questions.why: Boiling dulls mustard's bite and can make it bitter, so it goes in at the end and the sauce is not boiled again.

questions.q: The mustard cream on the Brennan's Poussin à la Moutarde follows which French classic?
questions.answer: Poulet à la moutarde, the Burgundian bistro chicken
distractors: Steak au poivre, flamed with cognac
Sole meunière, in brown butter
Coq au vin, braised in red wine
questions.why: It follows poulet à la moutarde: shallot, white wine and cream, with the mustard stirred in off the heat, here over a sweet tea-brined, fried Cornish hen.

entries.title: Monter au beurre
entries.summary: To mount a sauce with butter: cold butter swirled or whisked into a hot sauce, off the boil, at the last moment, for gloss, body and a rounder taste. Simple to do and easy to undo, because a sauce that reboils breaks.
entries.guest: A sauce finished with butter has a little cold butter swirled in just before it comes to you, which gives it its shine and a softer, rounder taste.

paras: Monter au beurre means to mount with butter: cold butter swirled or whisked into a hot sauce, off the boil, just before it goes to the plate. Monter is French for to go up or to mount, and kitchens use it for building anything up. Butter is about four-fifths fat, the rest mostly water with a little milk protein. Swirled in cold and in pieces, it does not simply melt but breaks into fine droplets held in the sauce's water: a light emulsion.

It gives gloss, a little body, a rounder taste that softens the edge of wine and acid, and richness from a small amount. It is the last touch on a great many brown sauces and pan sauces, and the difference between a dull sauce and one that shines at the pass.

Cut unsalted butter, straight from the fridge, into dice of about 1 to 2 cm (1/2 to 3/4 inch). Bring the sauce to the right body first, since butter thickens it only by a shade. Take the pan off the heat so it stops bubbling. Add a few pieces and swirl or whisk gently until they have almost gone, then add more. Keep the sauce moving, hot but below the simmer, roughly 70 to 80°C (158 to 176°F). Taste, season and send it.

Mount at the last moment. A mounted sauce waits only briefly, warm but off direct heat, and goes out within minutes, never longer than the chef's own standard allows. Never reboil it: the fat droplets run together, and the sauce thins, dulls and floats a slick of oil. A sauce built on a stock rich in gelatine mounts readily and holds longer, because gelatine thickens the water around the droplets and helps keep them apart.

A dependable measure is 30 to 60 g (1 to 2 oz) of cold butter for each 240 ml (1 cup) of sauce, an eighth to a quarter of its weight. Less gives shine without richness; much more makes a butter sauce that tastes of little else and breaks at the first knock.

Three butter preparations are easily confused. Mounting finishes a sauce that already exists: the sauce is the body and a little butter the polish. In a beurre blanc, butter is most of the sauce, whisked into a few spoonfuls of reduced wine, vinegar and shallot. A beurre monté is butter emulsified into a little boiling water, a neutral butter for poaching, glazing and holding food moist at the pass. Each has its own entry.

On the stove, a cook mounts a red wine jus, a light sauce of meat juices and wine, just before plating. A deglazed pan sauce is mounted once it reaches nappe, thick enough to coat a spoon. A classical marchand de vin, shallot and red wine reduced and then simmered with demi-glace, a rich brown sauce, is commonly finished with butter. Whether a house sauce such as Brennan's marchand de vin is finished this way is the kitchen's to say. A cream sauce often needs little or none.

Greasy beads or a ring of oil: too hot, or boiled after mounting. Off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of cold water or cold stock, which can pull a lightly broken sauce back; a fully split one is skimmed, brought back to nappe and mounted afresh. Dull and thin: the butter went in soft or all at once. Greasy however long you whisk: too little gelatine in the stock. Set at the edges: held too cool, so warm it gently, never to the boil.

Escoffier's Guide Culinaire, first published in 1903, finishes sauce after sauce with butter added off the fire. Later, the nouvelle cuisine of the 1960s and 1970s turned away from heavy flour-thickened sauces in favour of lighter reductions, and a reduction finished with a little butter remains a familiar restaurant sauce.

Guests seldom hear the French; a menu may say finished with butter, or simply a glossy jus. Describe the sauce, not the technique: a red wine sauce with a silky finish. Send the plate quickly, because a mounted sauce dulls as it waits. A butter finish changes the answer to a guest's question about butter or milk, so that question goes to the kitchen.

faults.fault: Greasy beads or a ring of oil
faults.cause: The sauce was too hot when the butter went in, or boiled after mounting.
faults.fix: Off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of cold water or cold stock; if fully split, skim, bring back to nappe and mount afresh.

faults.cause: The butter went in soft or all at once and melted into a pool.
faults.fix: Use cold diced butter, a few pieces at a time, swirling until each has almost gone.

faults.fault: Will not take the butter, stays greasy
faults.cause: A stock with too little gelatine.
faults.fix: Reduce the base further, or build it on a gelatine-rich stock next time.
Warm it gently, whisking, and never let it reach the boil.

cards.front: What does monter au beurre mean?
cards.back: To mount with butter: cold butter swirled or whisked into a hot sauce, off the boil, at the last moment before it is served.

cards.front: What does mounting with butter give a sauce?
cards.back: Gloss, a little more body, a rounder taste that softens wine and acid, and richness from a small amount of butter.

cards.front: Why must the butter be cold and in pieces?
cards.back: Cold pieces melt slowly as the pan is swirled, so the fat breaks into fine droplets in the sauce instead of melting into a pool that separates.

cards.front: How hot should the sauce be when the butter goes in?
cards.back: Hot but below the simmer, roughly 70 to 80°C (158 to 176°F), with the pan off the heat or at the edge of the stove.

cards.front: What happens if a mounted sauce comes back to the boil?
cards.back: The droplets of fat run together: the sauce thins, turns dull and floats a slick of oil.

cards.front: How much butter mounts a sauce?
cards.back: About 30 to 60 g (1 to 2 oz) of cold butter for each 240 ml (1 cup) of finished sauce, an eighth to a quarter of its weight.

cards.front: Why does a sauce built on a gelatine-rich stock mount better?
cards.back: Gelatine thickens the water around the butter droplets and helps keep them apart, so the sauce takes the butter readily and holds longer.

cards.front: A mounted sauce has just begun to look greasy. What is the first fix?
cards.back: Off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of cold water or cold stock. If it has fully split, skim it, bring it back to nappe and mount it afresh.

cards.front: How does mounting a sauce differ from making a beurre blanc?
cards.back: Mounting adds a little butter to finish a sauce that already exists; in a beurre blanc the butter is most of the sauce, whisked into a small reduction.

cards.front: How does a beurre monté differ from a mounted sauce?
cards.back: Beurre monté is butter emulsified into a little boiling water, a neutral cooking and holding medium; a mounted sauce is a finished sauce with some butter added.

cards.front: When is a sauce mounted, and how long can it wait?
cards.back: At the last moment before plating. It waits only briefly, somewhere warm and off direct heat, and goes out within minutes, never longer than the chef's own standard allows.

cards.front: How do you describe a butter-finished sauce to a guest?
cards.back: Describe the sauce, not the technique: a red wine sauce with a silky finish. Any question about butter or milk goes to the kitchen.

questions.q: What does a cook do to monter au beurre?
questions.answer: Swirl cold butter into a hot sauce, off the boil
distractors: Brown butter in the pan until it smells of hazelnuts
Cook butter and flour into a roux
Clarify butter to remove its water
questions.why: Mounting is the finish: cold butter added in pieces to a hot sauce that is no longer boiling, just before service.

questions.q: Why is the butter for mounting used cold and in pieces?
questions.answer: It melts slowly and disperses as fine droplets
distractors: Cold butter carries more salt
It cools the sauce enough to serve
It keeps the sauce from reducing any further in the pan
questions.why: Melting slowly while the pan is swirled, the butter breaks into droplets held in the sauce, instead of a pool of fat that separates.

questions.q: Roughly how hot should a sauce be while it is mounted with butter?
distractors: 100°C (212°F), at a rolling boil
85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F), at a simmer
questions.why: Hot but below the simmer: cooler and the butter sets, at a boil the droplets run together and the sauce breaks.

questions.q: A mounted red wine jus is put back on a high flame and boils. What happens?
questions.answer: It thins, dulls and floats a slick of oil
distractors: It thickens to a glaze and keeps its shine
The butter browns and turns it nutty
Nothing changes once butter is in
questions.why: Boiling makes the butter droplets merge, so the emulsion breaks; a mounted sauce is never reboiled.

questions.q: Which is a dependable measure of butter for mounting a sauce?
questions.answer: 30 to 60 g (1 to 2 oz) for each 240 ml (1 cup)
distractors: 5 g (1 tsp) for each 1 litre (about 1 quart)
500 g (1 lb) for each 240 ml (1 cup)
Equal weights of butter and sauce
questions.why: About an eighth to a quarter of the sauce's weight gives gloss and body; much more turns it into a fragile butter sauce.

questions.q: Why does a jus built on gelatine-rich veal stock take butter more readily?
questions.answer: Gelatine helps hold the butter droplets apart
distractors: Gelatine raises the boiling point of the sauce
Gelatine stops the butter melting
Veal stock is mostly fat already
questions.why: Gelatine thickens the water around each droplet, steadying the emulsion; a thin, gelatine-poor stock slicks instead of mounting.

questions.q: What separates mounting a sauce from making a beurre blanc?
questions.answer: In a beurre blanc, butter is most of the sauce
distractors: A beurre blanc is thickened with an egg yolk liaison
Mounting uses clarified butter only
A beurre blanc is boiled to finish it
questions.why: Mounting polishes a sauce that already exists; a beurre blanc is built from butter whisked into a small, sharp reduction, with no yolk.

questions.q: A mounted sauce has just begun to look greasy at the pass. What is the first fix?
questions.answer: Off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of cold water
distractors: Bring it back to a hard boil to tighten it up again
Whisk in a spoonful of flour off the heat
Whisk in more soft butter over the flame
questions.why: Cold water cools the sauce and gives the fat more water to disperse into, which can pull a lightly broken mount back.

entries.title: Flambé
entries.summary: Flambé means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so its vapour burns in a short burst of flame. It burns off some alcohol, never all, adds aroma and a touch of caramel, and gives the dining room a show.
entries.guest: Flambéed means flamed: the spirit is lit in the pan and burns for a few moments. The flame takes some of the alcohol, but not all of it.

paras: Flamber is French for to flame, and a dish served flambé has had spirit poured into a hot pan and lit. What burns is not the liquid but the alcohol vapour rising from it, which is why the flame dances above the pan and dies on its own once the vapour runs short, usually in well under a minute.

It burns off some of the alcohol, never all, and much stays in the sauce. The heat of the flame caramelises a little sugar on the surface and leaves the spirit's aroma softer and rounder than it was raw, a real but modest change. Much of the point is theatre, so much flambé is done in the dining room.

Strength matters. Spirits of around 40 per cent alcohol, such as brandy, cognac, dark rum and many orange liqueurs, light readily, especially when warm. Wine and fortified wine, at roughly 12 to 20 per cent, rarely catch in an ordinary pan. Overproof spirits, well above 50 per cent, flare high and fast and have no place on a busy line.

In the kitchen, measure the spirit into a small jug first, about 30 to 60 ml (2 to 4 tbsp) for a sauce for two; poured from the bottle near a flame, fire can travel back up the neck. Pull the pan off the flame and pour in the spirit. Return it and tilt the far edge towards the gas flame to light the vapour, or use a long match on induction. Stand back, a lid within reach to smother it, and let the flame burn out. In a bright room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until you are sure it has died, and turn the burner off before you step away.

The classics: steak au poivre, a pepper-crusted steak whose pan is often flamed with cognac and finished with cream; steak Diane, with shallot, mustard and cognac, long a tableside favourite; and the flamed desserts, crêpes Suzette with orange liqueur, cherries jubilee and Bananas Foster, each with its own entry.

A brandy and green peppercorn pan sauce shows the method at the stove. Sear and rest the steaks, pour off the fat, and sweat shallot with drained green peppercorns, the soft unripe berries kept in brine. Take the pan off the heat, add about 60 ml (1/4 cup) of brandy from a measure, light it and let it burn out. Add brown stock and reduce by half, add cream and simmer to nappe, then finish with cold butter off the heat.

Will not light: the spirit is too weak, too cold or too little, or the pan has cooled. Warm the pan briefly and tilt again; never add more spirit to a pan that may be alight. Flares too high: too much spirit, an overproof bottle, or spirit poured in over the flame; cover it with the lid. Harsh and boozy: the sauce was not reduced after the flame died, so simmer it longer. Bitter: the sugar or the fond was too dark beforehand.

Cherries jubilee is generally credited to Escoffier, for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be that of 1897; his version was served with warmed kirsch lit at the table, and no ice cream. In New Orleans the flame stayed in the dining room: Bananas Foster was created at Brennan's in 1951, while it was still Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré on Bourbon Street.

At Brennan's two desserts are flamed at the table on a guéridon, the tableside cart: the World Famous Bananas Foster, with rum, and the Cherries Jubilee, tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce over housemade vanilla ice cream. The house's tableside steps go beyond the kitchen method; they are learned word for word and taught in Flambé safety at the table. Who performs the flambé is a lineup question for the manager, and a new server never lights a pan before sign-off. The Jubilee was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026: confirm with a manager before offering it.

Say flahm-BAY, and flahm-BAYD for flambéed. Guests often ask whether the alcohol burns off: not all of it, and much stays in the sauce. For a guest who avoids alcohol, the guide steers to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. Which rum and spirit the kitchen uses are questions for the chef.

cards.front: What does flambé mean?
cards.back: Flamed: spirit is added to a hot pan and lit, so its alcohol vapour burns in a short burst of flame.

cards.front: What actually burns when a pan is flamed?
cards.back: The alcohol vapour rising above the liquid, not the liquid itself; the flame dies on its own once the vapour runs short.

cards.front: Does flaming burn off all the alcohol?
cards.back: No. It burns some of the vapour, but much of the alcohol stays in the sauce, so a guest who avoids alcohol is told so.

cards.front: Besides burning some alcohol, what does a flambé do?
cards.back: It caramelises a little sugar on the surface, softens and rounds the spirit's aroma, and gives the dining room a show.

cards.front: Which spirits light well, and which do not?
cards.back: Spirits around 40 per cent alcohol light readily; wine and fortified wine rarely catch, and overproof spirits flare dangerously high.

cards.front: Why is the spirit measured into a small jug first?
cards.back: Pouring from the bottle near a flame can carry fire back up the neck, and a measure also limits how big the flame can be.

cards.front: Why does the pan come off the flame before the spirit goes in?
cards.back: Over the flame the spirit can vaporise and ignite as it is poured; off the heat, the cook chooses the moment it lights.

cards.front: What is kept within reach whenever a pan is flamed, and why?
cards.back: A lid: covering the pan cuts off the air and smothers a flame that rises too high.

cards.front: Name the classic flambé dishes.
cards.back: Steak au poivre and steak Diane at the stove; crêpes Suzette, cherries jubilee and Bananas Foster among the desserts.

cards.front: What is the order of a brandy and green peppercorn pan sauce?
cards.back: Sear and rest the steak, pour off the fat, sweat shallot and peppercorns, add brandy off the heat and light it, then stock, cream, nappe and cold butter.

cards.front: The spirit will not light. What do you do?
cards.back: Warm the pan briefly back over the heat and tilt again; never add more spirit to a pan that may already be alight.

cards.front: Which Brennan's desserts are flamed at the table?
cards.back: The World Famous Bananas Foster, with rum, and the Cherries Jubilee in a Luxardo sauce; confirm the Jubilee with a manager before offering it.

questions.q: When a pan is flamed, what is actually burning?
questions.answer: The alcohol vapour above the liquid
distractors: The butter in the pan
The sugar in the sauce
The whole liquid, to the last drop
questions.why: Only the vapour burns, which is why the flame sits above the pan and dies on its own once the vapour runs short.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the flame burns off all the alcohol. What is true?
questions.answer: No, much of it stays in the sauce
distractors: Yes, every trace is gone
Yes, once the flame turns blue
Only rum stays; brandy burns away
questions.why: Only the vapour burns, and only while the flame lasts, so much of the alcohol stays in the sauce; a guest who avoids alcohol is told and offered another dessert.

questions.q: Which of these is the likeliest to light well in a hot pan?
questions.answer: Brandy at 40 per cent
distractors: Dry white wine at 12 per cent
Sherry at 17 per cent
Port at 20 per cent
questions.why: Spirits near 40 per cent give off enough vapour to catch; wines and fortified wines rarely do in an ordinary pan.

questions.q: Why is the spirit poured into a small jug before the pan is flamed?
questions.answer: Fire can travel back up the neck of a bottle
distractors: A jug warms the spirit to boiling
Spirit poured from the bottle is too strong to light
The jug burns off the alcohol first
questions.why: Pouring from the bottle near a flame risks fire running back into it; a measure also limits the size of the flame.

questions.q: At what moment does the spirit go into the pan?
questions.answer: With the pan pulled off the flame
distractors: While the pan sits over a high flame
Once the pan is already alight
After the cream has gone in
questions.why: Off the heat, the spirit is far less likely to ignite as it is poured; the pan goes back and is tilted so the cook chooses the moment it lights.

questions.q: The flame rises higher than expected. What should already be within reach?
questions.answer: A lid to cover the pan
distractors: A jug of water
A second measure of spirit
A ladle of cold stock
questions.why: A lid cuts off the air and smothers the flame; water thrown into a hot, fatty pan can spread the fire.

questions.q: Which of these is a classic flambé dish?
questions.answer: Steak au poivre
distractors: Sole meunière
Eggs Sardou
Bouillabaisse
questions.why: Steak au poivre's pan is often flamed with cognac before the cream; meunière is finished with brown butter, and the others are not flamed.

questions.q: Which two Brennan's desserts are flamed at the table?
questions.answer: Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee
distractors: Lemon Tart and Bread Pudding
Baked Apple and The Snickers
Blackberry Trifle and Tarte Tatin
questions.why: Both are flamed on the guéridon over vanilla ice cream; the Jubilee is confirmed with a manager first, as it was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026.
